title: Crane Over
description: A crane-over lifts and arcs the camera on a jib or crane until it looks down on the scene from above. Height and angle change together in one move, turning the floor into a map.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: The shot turns a scene into a diagram without cutting. Bodies, tables, and streets become plan view because the arm has climbed and pitched over them.
It is not a still overhead: the audience rides the change of rank. It is the wrong tool when you already want a locked top-down, or when a simple crane-up should keep looking forward at a skyline.
If you never reach a downward angle, you only craned up.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Boom up and arc forward, remote head tilting down as the arm passes over the subject. End nearly nadir or at a steep high angle.
Watch for the subject being covered by the arm's shadow and for changing key as you face new windows. Prompt a crane over, arm rising and arcing forward until the camera looks nearly straight down.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it to turn a scene into a map without cutting. Concrete beat: a dinner argument, then the table as a chessboard.
Do not crane over if the last frame is still a forward wide.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: A Crane Up typically keeps a forward look as it rises and eases back. An Overhead Top-Down can be a locked top-down with no ride.
A Jib Shot can do a small version of this arc over a table. Crane over is the continuous climb into downward view.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: The Untouchables uses crane height over the Union Station staircase so the action becomes a diagram of steps and bodies. Birdman rides theater space until floor plans and faces share one path.
Use the arc-into-down, not the period costumes.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Crane over [Subject], the arm rising and arcing forward until the camera looks nearly straight down, a continuous climb into overhead. For motion: the camera cranes up and over [Subject], finishing in a high downward angle.
The camera cranes up and over [Subject], finishing in a high downward angle.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is a Crane Up that never looks down, or a cut to Overhead Top-Down. The tell is a forward skyline at the end, or a jump to top-down.
The fix: one arm path that finishes steeply downward, subject still readable as a map.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is Crane Over in film?
It is a crane move that rises and arcs until the camera looks down, combining a height change with a change of angle in one path.
Crane Over vs Crane Up
Crane up usually eases back while still looking across the world. Crane over continues until the view is downward and the floor becomes the picture.
When should I use Crane Over?
When blocking should become a map without a cut. Do not use it if you wanted a skyline or a still overhead lock-off.
How do I prompt Crane Over for AI image or video?
Write crane up and over [Subject], finishing nearly straight down. One continuous arm move. Ban a cut to top-down.
